questions.title: Definition of pharmacodynamics
questions.question: The pharmacodynamics are defined as:

options.A: The effect of the environment has on our bodies
options.B: The effect of the kidney on drug molecules
options.C: The effect a drug has on our bodies
options.D: The effect our body has on drugs

explanations.A: Incorrect. "The effect of the environment on our bodies" describes neither branch of pharmacology taught here; it is not a recognised definition of pharmacodynamics, and confusing it with the drug-body relationship is a distractor, not a real alternative teaching point.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Renal handling of a drug is a pharmacokinetic detail (part of excretion), not a definition of pharmacodynamics, and it describes one organ's role in drug elimination rather than the drug's own effect on the body as a whole.
explanations.C: Correct. Pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body: the receptors it occupies, the effect it produces, and how that effect grows with concentration. This is the mirror-image half of pharmacokinetics, which instead asks what the body does to the drug (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion). Getting the direction right -- drug acting on body, versus body acting on drug -- is the single fact this whole vocabulary pair turns on.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "The effect our body has on drugs" is the definition of pharmacokinetics, not pharmacodynamics -- this option reverses the direction of action that distinguishes the two terms.

questions.learning_objective: Define pharmacodynamics as the drug's effect on the body, distinct from pharmacokinetics (the body's effect on the drug).

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: The effect a drug has on our bodies"

questions.title: Pharmacodynamics as the study of drug action
questions.question: Pharmacodynamics can be defined as the study of:

explanations.A: Correct. Pharmacodynamics is the study of drug action -- what the drug does to the body, including the receptors it occupies and the effect it produces. Restated as "the study of drug action" rather than as a full sentence definition, this is the same pharmacokinetics-versus-pharmacodynamics distinction tested elsewhere in this quiz, phrased differently. A student who can state the PK/PD split in either wording has the concept.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Biotransformation is another name for drug metabolism, one of the four pharmacokinetic phases (what the body does to the drug), not a definition of pharmacodynamics.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Absorption is the first of the four pharmacokinetic phases -- a drug's movement into the bloodstream -- not the study of drug action at its receptor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Distribution is the second pharmacokinetic phase -- a drug's movement from blood into tissues -- not a definition of pharmacodynamics.

questions.learning_objective: Restate pharmacodynamics as the study of drug action, and distinguish it from the three named pharmacokinetic phases offered as distractors.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Drug action"

questions.title: Definition of pharmacokinetics
questions.question: The pharmacokinetics are defined as:

options.A: The effect our body has on drugs
options.B: The effect a drug has on our bodies
options.C: The effect of the kidney on drug molecules
options.D: The effect of the environment has on our bodies

explanations.A: Correct. Pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug: its absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion, which together determine the concentration reaching the site of action. This is the mirror-image half of pharmacodynamics, which instead asks what the drug does to the body. The two terms are deliberately paired in this teaching set so a student learns to sort a fact into one or the other by asking which direction the action runs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "The effect a drug has on our bodies" is the definition of pharmacodynamics, not pharmacokinetics -- this option reverses the direction of action that distinguishes the two terms.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Renal handling of a drug is only one part of the excretion phase within pharmacokinetics, not a definition of the whole discipline.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "The effect of the environment on our bodies" is not a recognised definition of either pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics; it names neither the drug-on-body nor body-on-drug relationship this vocabulary pair distinguishes.

questions.learning_objective: Define pharmacokinetics as the body's effect on the drug, distinct from pharmacodynamics (the drug's effect on the body).

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: The effect our body has on drugs"

questions.title: Competitive vs non-competitive antagonism: potency and efficacy
questions.question: A competitive antagonist affects the agonist's --------- and a non-competitive antagonist affects the agonist's ----------

explanations.A: Incorrect. Duration and speed are not the two properties this classic pharmacodynamics pair distinguishes; a competitive antagonist's effect is described by a rightward shift of the dose-response curve (potency), not a change in how fast or how long the agonist acts.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses the correct pairing: a competitive antagonist is the one that reduces potency (shifting the curve right), while a non-competitive antagonist is the one that reduces efficacy (flattening the maximum response), not the other way round.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Speed and duration are not the properties tested; the standard teaching pair for competitive versus non-competitive antagonism is potency and efficacy, read from the shape of the shifted concentration-response curve.
explanations.D: Correct. A competitive antagonist binds the same site as the agonist, so enough agonist can displace it: the concentration-response curve shifts to the right in parallel, reducing potency, while the maximum response is eventually still reached. A non-competitive antagonist binds elsewhere (or binds irreversibly), so agonist cannot displace it: the curve's maximum falls, reducing efficacy, and no amount of agonist restores it. Potency for competitive, efficacy for non-competitive is the pairing this teaching point isolates.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish competitive antagonism (reduces potency) from non-competitive antagonism (reduces efficacy) by the property of the agonist's dose-response curve each one changes.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Potency, Efficacy"

questions.title: Definition of an antagonist
questions.question: An antagonist is a substance that:

options.A: Binds to the receptors without directly altering their functions
options.B: Binds to the receptors and initiates changes in cell function, producing maximal effect
options.C: Interacts with plasma proteins and does not produce any effect
options.D: Binds to the receptors and initiates changes in cell function, producing submaximal effect

explanations.A: Correct. An antagonist binds a receptor with affinity but has no efficacy of its own: it does not initiate the conformational change that produces a cellular response, and acts only by occupying the receptor and preventing an agonist from binding there. An antagonist alone at a quiet receptor does nothing at all -- what looks like an effect when an antagonist is given is really the removal of agonist tone that was already present, not a new action of its own.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Binding a receptor and producing a maximal effect is the definition of a full agonist, not an antagonist -- an antagonist by definition produces no effect of its own on binding.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Plasma protein binding is a drug-distribution phenomenon (part of pharmacokinetics), not the definition of a pharmacodynamic antagonist, which specifically concerns receptor binding, not protein binding in the blood.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Binding a receptor and producing a submaximal effect describes a partial agonist, which does have some efficacy, not an antagonist, which has none.

questions.title: Definition of a full agonist
questions.question: If an agonist can produce maximal effects and has high efficacy it's called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Agonist-antagonist" is not the term for a high-efficacy ligand producing a maximal response; that mixed-behaviour label is more commonly applied to drugs that act as an agonist at one receptor subtype and an antagonist at another, not to a simple maximal-effect ligand.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A partial agonist produces a submaximal response however much is given -- the opposite of the maximal, high-efficacy response this question describes -- and in the presence of a full agonist it can even act as a relative antagonist.
explanations.C: Correct. A full agonist binds the receptor and produces the maximum response the receptor can give, i.e. it has high (maximal) efficacy. This is the reference point against which a partial agonist (submaximal response, lower efficacy) is defined and compared.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An antagonist binds with affinity but has no efficacy of its own and produces no direct effect -- the opposite of the maximal-effect ligand described here.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a full agonist as a ligand producing the maximal, high-efficacy response a receptor can give.

questions.title: Definition of a partial agonist
questions.question: If an agonist can produce submaximal effects and has moderate efficacy it's called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. An antagonist has no efficacy of its own and produces no response at all -- the opposite of the moderate, submaximal response this question describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A full agonist produces the maximal response the receptor can give, i.e. high efficacy, whatever the dose -- the opposite of the submaximal, moderate-efficacy response described here.
explanations.C: Correct. A partial agonist binds with affinity but produces only a submaximal response however much is given, reflecting moderate rather than maximal efficacy. In the presence of a full agonist, a partial agonist can even act as a relative antagonist, since it competes for the same receptor while producing a weaker effect than the full agonist would alone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Agonist-antagonist" more commonly describes a drug with mixed activity across different receptor subtypes, not the single, submaximal-efficacy behaviour at one receptor described here.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a partial agonist as a ligand producing a submaximal, moderate-efficacy response, and note its antagonist-like behaviour alongside a full agonist.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Partial agonist"

questions.title: Definition of intrinsic activity
questions.question: Intrinsic activity is a drug's ability to elicit:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Excretion is a pharmacokinetic process (drug removal from the body), unrelated to intrinsic activity, which is a pharmacodynamic property describing what happens once a drug binds its receptor.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Weak receptor binding describes affinity, not intrinsic activity -- affinity is the tendency of a drug to bind and hold onto a receptor, which says nothing about whether the bound drug then produces any effect.
explanations.C: Correct. Intrinsic activity is a drug's ability to elicit a response once bound to its receptor. It is what separates a full agonist (high intrinsic activity, maximal response) from a partial agonist (lower intrinsic activity, submaximal response) and from an antagonist (zero intrinsic activity, no response at all). This holds independent of how tightly any of the three binds, since affinity and intrinsic activity are two separate properties.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Strong receptor binding also describes affinity, not intrinsic activity -- a drug can bind very tightly (high affinity) and still have zero intrinsic activity, which is exactly the definition of an antagonist.

questions.learning_objective: Define intrinsic activity as a ligand's ability to produce a response once bound, and distinguish it from affinity (the tendency to bind).

questions.title: Definition of an agonist
questions.question: Which one of the following statements describes an agonist?

options.A: A drug that binds to a receptor and stimulates cellular activity
options.B: A specific regulatory molecule in the biologic system where a drug interacts
options.C: A drug that increases concentration of another drug at receptor sites
options.D: A drug that binds to a receptor but does not produce intrinsic activity

explanations.A: Correct. An agonist is a drug that binds to a receptor and stimulates cellular activity -- it has both affinity (it binds) and intrinsic activity (the binding produces a response). This is the general definition covering both full and partial agonists, who differ only in how much response (efficacy) their binding produces, not in whether they produce a response at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "A specific regulatory molecule in the biologic system where a drug interacts" describes a receptor itself, not an agonist -- the receptor is what an agonist binds to, not the agonist.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Increasing the concentration of another drug at receptor sites is not the definition of an agonist; no standard pharmacodynamic term is defined this way, and it confuses a drug's own receptor action with a pharmacokinetic interaction between two drugs.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Binding a receptor without producing intrinsic activity is the definition of an antagonist, not an agonist -- an agonist is specifically defined by producing a response, the opposite of this option.

questions.learning_objective: State the general definition of an agonist (binds a receptor and stimulates cellular activity), covering both full and partial agonists.
